name: Sharif
definition: Sharif is a composite portrait of a Muslim working-class man from Manvi taluk in Raichur district, employed in the stone-crushing industry along the Tungabhadra Left Bank Canal command. He represents the mix of irrigated-agriculture opportunity and quarry-labour risk that shapes livelihoods in this corner of Kalyana Karnataka.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Sharif loads crushed stone onto tractors at a small quarry near Manvi town, earning around eight thousand rupees a month when work is steady. During the irrigation season he also drives a tractor for a local farmer who grows paddy on ten acres under the Tungabhadra Left Bank Canal, adding another three to four thousand rupees across those months. The quarry work is dusty and hard on his chest; he coughs often and has heard older workers talk about silicosis, though he has never been screened for it. The tractor-driving brings him into the canal-command paddy belt where water flows predictably, unlike the dryland cotton and jowar patches further from the canal. His income is seasonal and unpredictable: the quarry shuts when orders drop and the tractor work lasts only as long as the canal runs. He leaves home before dawn, returns after dark, and spends Fridays at the mosque in Manvi town. Economic pressure is constant; every month he calculates what is left after rent, groceries and his children's school fees.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Sharif lives with his wife Naseema, their two sons aged ten and seven, and his widowed mother in a rented two-room house on the edge of Manvi town. Naseema stitches blouses and petticoats at home for a local tailor, earning around two thousand rupees a month, and manages all the household cooking, cleaning and caregiving. His mother, in her sixties, helps mind the younger boy when Naseema is busy with orders. Sharif's father died five years ago from a heart attack; there was no insurance and the family borrowed heavily for the funeral. Sharif himself married at twenty-two, shortly after his father arranged the match with Naseema's family from a village near Sindhanur. Gender roles are traditional: Naseema does not work outside the home, and Sharif makes all major financial decisions. He worries about finding enough money for his sons' future—both their schooling now and, later, their marriages. His mother receives a widow's pension of six hundred rupees a month, which helps with groceries but covers little else.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: Sharif studied until Class 7 in a government Urdu-medium school in Manvi, then dropped out to help his father with farm labour. He can read Urdu script and simple Kannada, and speaks Dakhni Urdu at home and broken Kannada at work. His two sons attend the government Urdu-medium primary school in Manvi town, walking fifteen minutes each way. The school is free under the RTE Act, but Sharif pays for books, uniforms and the boys' mid-day snacks, totalling around fifteen hundred rupees a year. He dreams of keeping them in school through SSLC and perhaps into a diploma course, ideally something that leads to a government job under the Article 371(J) local quota that everyone talks about. His wife, who studied only until Class 5, insists the boys must study further than their parents did. The older boy is bright and enjoys school; the younger one is less interested and sometimes skips classes to play cricket.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: Sharif's persistent cough worries him, but he has never visited a doctor for it because the nearest government hospital is in Raichur town, an hour away by bus, and he cannot afford to lose a day's wages. His wife once suggested he get a chest X-ray, but he dismissed it as too expensive. Naseema and the boys are generally healthy, though the younger son had a bad fever last year and they spent two thousand rupees at a private clinic in Manvi for tests and medicines. His mother has joint pain and mild diabetes, managed with tablets from a local pharmacy; she has never seen a specialist. The family drinks water from a borewell shared with neighbours; Sharif has heard talk of fluoride in the groundwater in some parts of Raichur district, but does not know if it affects Manvi. They are enrolled in Ayushman Bharat, but Sharif is unclear about what it covers and has never tried to use it. Dust from the quarry settles in his lungs and on his skin; he knows men who have collapsed at work, but no one has ever explained silicosis to him in detail. Healthcare feels distant and costly, something to avoid unless absolutely necessary.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: Sharif is Muslim, part of the substantial Muslim population in Raichur district with roots going back to the Hyderabad State period. He prays five times a day when work allows, always attends Friday prayers at the Jama Masjid in Manvi town, and observes Ramadan strictly. His family speaks Dakhni Urdu at home, the everyday language of Muslims in this part of Kalyana Karnataka, though he uses Kannada when dealing with quarry supervisors and tractor owners. The mosque is a social hub: after prayers he discusses work, water shortages and children's schooling with other men. He respects the Khwaja Bande Nawaz Dargah in Kalaburagi, though he has visited it only twice in his life. His neighbourhood in Manvi is mixed—Muslims, Lingayats and Scheduled Castes—but socialising mostly stays within community lines. He feels a strong sense of Muslim identity and is alert to any slight or exclusion, though he does not talk about it much. Naseema and his mother fast, cook for Eid and maintain strict halal practice. Sharif sees himself as a believer and a provider, trying to live a decent life in difficult circumstances.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: He knows about Article 371(J) special status and the local-job reservation it promises, and he pins his hopes on it for his sons' future. He hears people talk about the Kalyana Karnataka Regional Development Board and funds that are supposed to come to the region, but he has not seen any direct benefit—no new roads, no better school buildings in Manvi. He receives Anna Bhagya rations every month, ten kilograms of rice that he collects from the ration shop without fail. His wife uses the Shakti free-bus scheme to visit her parents in Sindhanur, saving the family a few hundred rupees a month. Sharif has never dealt with the taluk office or applied for any scheme beyond his ration card and Ayushman card. He is wary of officials, whom he sees as indifferent or corrupt. He knows the local corporator by sight but has never approached him. Government feels distant, something that announces programs but delivers little to men like him.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: Sharif worries most about money—whether there will be quarry work next month, whether the tractor owner will call him, whether he can keep paying school fees. He is proud of working hard and staying honest, and he resents the stereotype that Muslims are backward or uneducated; he points to his sons' schooling as proof that his family is trying. He feels Kalyana Karnataka has been neglected by the state government for decades, left behind while Bengaluru and the south prosper, and he is glad the region finally has Article 371(J), even if he does not yet see much change. He blames quarry owners for not caring about workers' lungs, blames the irrigation department when the canal runs dry too early, and blames middlemen for cheating farmers. He is frustrated that people assume Dakhni Urdu speakers are not "real" Kannadigas, when his family has lived here for generations. He dreams of his sons getting government jobs under the local quota, marrying well, and living more securely than he does. He rarely complains out loud, but he carries a steady, low-level anger at how hard everything is.
